title: Investigation of acoustic comfort, productivity, and engagement in naturally ventilated university classrooms: Role of background noise and students' noise sensitivity

findings.mechanism: higher BGN levels are associated with lower acoustic environment acceptability
findings.quote: statistically significant association of acoustic environment acceptability with BGNLAeq-DL [ x²(10) = 20.3, p = .026]

findings.mechanism: longer RT is associated with lower acoustic environment acceptability
higher SNR is associated with higher acoustic environment acceptability
students are more likely to accept the acoustic environment when BGN is below this threshold

findings.mechanism: higher BGN levels reduce perceived acoustic comfort
findings.quote: BGN level (β = -0.085, p < .001) and NSS (β = -0.053, p = .002), significantly affect the perception towards acoustic comfort.

findings.mechanism: higher noise sensitivity leads to lower perceived acoustic comfort
findings.quote: BGN level (β = -0.085, p < .001) and NSS (β = -0.053, p = .002), significantly affect the perception towards acoustic comfort.

findings.antecedent: High Noise Sensitivity Score (NSS) and BGNLAeq-DL exceeded 62.4 dBA
findings.mechanism: individuals with high noise sensitivity experience discomfort at lower BGN thresholds
findings.quote: students with high noise sensitivity reported acoustic discomfort (ACV<0) after the 62.4 dBA level

findings.mechanism: longer RT reduces perceived acoustic comfort
findings.quote: RTocc level (β = -0.274, p = .004) and NSS (β = -0.053, p = .005), significantly affect the perception towards acoustic comfort.

findings.mechanism: higher noise sensitivity leads to lower perceived acoustic comfort, especially with longer RT
findings.quote: RTocc level (β = -0.274, p = .004) and NSS (β = -0.053, p = .005), significantly affect the perception towards acoustic comfort.

findings.antecedent: High Noise Sensitivity Score (NSS) and RTocc above 1.7 s
findings.mechanism: individuals with high noise sensitivity experience discomfort at longer RTs
findings.quote: students with high noise sensitivity did not report acoustic discomfort till an RTocc of 1.7 s.

findings.mechanism: higher SNR (lower e-SNR) leads to higher acoustic comfort
findings.quote: transformed SNR (ẞ = -6.392, p < .001) and NSS (β = -0.049, p = .007), significantly affect the perception towards acoustic comfort.

findings.mechanism: higher noise sensitivity leads to lower perceived acoustic comfort, especially with lower SNR
findings.quote: transformed SNR (ẞ = -6.392, p < .001) and NSS (β = -0.049, p = .007), significantly affect the perception towards acoustic comfort.

findings.antecedent: High Noise Sensitivity Score (NSS) and SNR below 3.7 dBA
findings.mechanism: individuals with high noise sensitivity experience discomfort at lower SNRs
findings.quote: students with high noise sensitivity did not report comfort (ACV>0) until the SNR reached 3.7 dBA.

findings.mechanism: SNR is the most influential acoustic feature for predicting comfort
findings.quote: random forest analysis identified component 2 as the most influential feature for predicting acoustic comfort, accounting for 34.8% of the model's predictive power

findings.mechanism: BGN is the second most influential acoustic feature for predicting comfort
findings.quote: followed by component 1 and component 3, which contributed 32.9% and 32.3%, respectively.

findings.mechanism: RT is the third most influential acoustic feature for predicting comfort
findings.quote: followed by component 1 and component 3, which contributed 32.9% and 32.3%, respectively.

stimuli.description: 11 naturally ventilated university classrooms with varying sizes, furniture arrangements, and ceiling fan configurations.

limitations: Data collection in some classrooms involved conducting measurements more than two times, with some variations in student groups across these sessions. On the other hand, some classrooms were only measured once due to the limited availability of lecture slots appropriate for the survey.
